newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Coffee nations fear consumer backlash.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Coffee nations fear consumer backlash.

text.p: Coffee producing nations led by Brazil began London talks on Monday to see if there is anything they can do to stabilize a wild international market.

The worry within the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) is that a speculative bubble in prices - one U.S. futures contract hit a 20-year high last week - may erode demand for coffee as people drink tea or soft drinks instead.
Some of the 14 members want to suspend export quotas.
"It is not logical to keep the quota system right now," the chief delegate of Costa Rica, Ricardo Seevers, told reporters.
But market analysts said that such a move may be mostly symbolic because, with coffee on the longest unbroken rally in two decades, nobody is expected to honour their quotes.

As the talks began, London futures for robusta coffee beans extended the advance that has seen prices roughly double since 1997 began. The London July contract rose $135 to $2,190 per tonne before easing slightly. A volatile mix of factors - low stocks, tight supply from Colombia and fears that Brazil, the biggest exporter, may have another frost - has lured speculators to the futures markets.

Last week saw U.S. spot May futures for better-quality arabica beans trade at $2.80 per pound, the highest since 1977. July, a more representative contract opened Monday at $2.55. The ACPC accounts for about 75 percent of world output. Quota rules aim to cap its exports at 25.5 million bags in the first half of 1997 but it now has to decide policy for beyond June 30.

The coffee talks began in a technical group of Brazil, Colombia, Ivory Coast, Indonesia, Uganda and El Salvador to put forward proposals for a full meeting on Wednesday. The attitude of Brazil may be crucial to any decisions. But the Brazilian president of the ACPC, Rubens Barbosa, declined to make any immediate comment to reporters.
A Uganda delegate said at the lunchtime adjournment that discussion was "lively". The ACPC secretary-general, Roberio Oliveira Silva, said 1997-98 crop forecasts were being examined.
London brokerage GNI Ltd noted in a commentary that several ACPC states sought an end to export quotas.

"If this was achieved," it added "Do not expect the market to collapse. It is hard to think of one producing country which is even thinking about adhering to its quota...market mechanisms have superseded any kind of export restraint..."
"Realistically what traders should be concerned about is what price level the ACPC feel is a fair floor to put under the market for next season," GNI said.
The French and British were last Friday the latest among consumers to be stung by new price rises in the shops.
Douwe Egberts France, owned by Sara Lee Corp, said this year's French retail increases on its arabica coffees now totalled around 45 percent.
French Cafes Excella SA said it planned new retail prices rises in June. But marketing director Jean-Jacques Dothee said he did not believe that futures reflected supply/demand fundamentals.
"There is no risk of a coffee shortage. We are being held hostage by a speculative game..." he said.
Dothee also gave a warning that high prices might scare away consumers, notably young people switching to soft drinks.
